nameStory: This tiny sea snail doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its scientific name, Propebela harpularia. The species name 'harpularia' comes from the Latin word for a small harp or harpoon, likely referring to the shell's elongated, pointed shape that resembles these ancient tools.
description: Propebela harpularia is a small sea snail that lives in New England's coastal waters. Like other marine snails, it carries a spiral shell on its back and moves along the seafloor using a muscular foot. These tiny mollusks are part of a large group called gastropods, which includes everything from garden snails to colorful sea slugs. They're quite small and easily overlooked by casual beachcombers.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: The shell is elongated and pointed, resembling a tiny tower or cone with a sharp spire that tapers to a fine point

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small, easily fitting on your fingernail - most shells you'll find are less than half an inch long

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: The shell surface feels smooth when dry, with fine spiral ridges that you can detect by running your finger gently along the surface

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Usually pale or whitish, sometimes with a slight yellowish or grayish tint, appearing almost translucent when fresh

idTips.label: Habitat Context
idTips.description: Found in deeper waters rather than the intertidal zone, so shells are typically discovered washed up on beaches rather than on living animals

habitat: This species lives in the deeper, cooler waters off New England's coast, typically beyond where most people swim or wade. You're most likely to encounter empty shells that have washed ashore on sandy or rocky beaches after storms. Look for them among other small shells and sea debris in the wrack line where waves deposit marine treasures.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells may wash ashore more frequently as spring storms churn up the seafloor and bring deep-water specimens to the surface.
seasonality.summer: Living specimens are active in deeper waters, but beachcombers might find weathered shells mixed with other marine debris during calm periods.
seasonality.fall: Storm activity increases the chances of finding fresh shells on beaches, especially after nor'easters that stir up offshore sediments.
seasonality.winter: Winter storms provide the best opportunities for shell collecting, as powerful waves bring material from deeper waters onto New England beaches.

funFact: This little snail is so rare in New England waters that it's only been officially documented twice in our region - making it one of the most elusive marine creatures you could possibly find while beachcombing!
confusionNotes: This species can be confused with other small, pointed marine snail shells found on New England beaches. The key is the very elongated, tower-like shape - if the shell looks more like a tiny ice cream cone than a broad spiral, you might have found something special.
contextualKnowledge: Scientists aren't entirely sure about this species' exact classification - you might see it listed under different genus names like Oenopota in older field guides or websites. This naming confusion is common with marine mollusks as researchers continue to study their relationships and revise classifications.
compareHints: Since this is the only Propebela species documented in New England, compare it to other small marine snails in the Mangeliidae family by looking for the distinctly elongated, pointed shell shape. Most other small sea snails in our region have broader, more rounded shells, while Propebela harpularia maintains that characteristic narrow, tower-like profile that sets it apart from its relatives.
